{{marriage|[[Joyce Brabner]]|1984|2010|end=his death}} | children = (foster child) Danielle Batone }} '''Harvey Lawrence Pekar''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|p|iː|k|ɑr}}; October 8, 1939 – July 12, 2010) was an American [[Underground comics|underground comic book]] writer, music critic, and media personality, best known for his autobiographical ''[[American Splendor]]'' comic series. In 2003, the series inspired a well-received [[American Splendor (film)|film adaptation]] of the same name. Frequently described as the "poet laureate of Cleveland,"{{cite web|url=http://blog.travelchannel.com/anthony-bourdain/read/the-original-goodbye-splendor/|title=The Original (Goodbye Splendor)|author=Bourdain, Anthony|authorlink=Anthony Bourdain|publisher=[[Travel Channel]]|date=July 13, 2010}}"[http://www.tabletmag.com/scroll/39242/harvey-pekar-dies Harvey Pekar Dies: Comic book writer was 'poet laureate of Cleveland']" by Marc Tracy, Tablet, July 12, 2010 Pekar "helped change the appreciation for, and perceptions of, the graphic novel, the drawn memoir, the autobiographical comic narrative.""[https://www.washingtonpost.com/blogs/comic-riffs/post/harvey-pekar-remembering-the-man--and-legacy--one-year-later/2011/07/13/gIQAbqodCI_blog.html HARVEY PEKAR: Remembering the man — and legacy — one year later]" by Michael Cavna, The Washington Post, 7/13/2011 Pekar described his work as "autobiography written as it's happening. The theme is about staying alive, getting a job, finding a mate, having a place to live, finding a creative outlet. Life is a [[attrition warfare|war of attrition]]. You have to stay active on all fronts. It's one thing after another. I've tried to control a chaotic universe. And it's a losing battle. But I can't let go. I've tried, but I can't."[https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/obituaries/culture-obituaries/books-obituaries/7888494/Harvey-Pekar.html "Harvey Pekar"] (obituary), ''[[The Daily Telegraph]]'', July 13, 2010 ==Life== Harvey Pekar and his younger brother Allen were born in [[Cleveland]], Ohio to Saul and Dora Pekar, immigrants from [[Białystok]], Poland. Saul Pekar was a [[Talmud]]ic scholar who owned a grocery store on Kinsman Avenue, with the family living above the store. While Pekar said he wasn't close to his parents due to their dissimilar backgrounds and because they worked all the time, he still "marveled at how devoted they were to each other. They had so much love and admiration for one another."{{cite book | title = Cleveland | first= Harvey | last= Pekar | first2= Joseph (illustrations) | last2= Remnant | publisher = Zip Comics and Top Shelf Productions | year= 2012 | page= 53}} As a child, Pekar's first language was [[Yiddish]], and he learned to read and appreciate novels in the language.{{cite web|url=http://heebmagazine.com/harvey-pekars-yiddishkeit-exclusive-art-and-comix/34706 |title=Exclusive: A Smorgasbord of Art and Comics Celebrating Harvey Pekar’s Yiddishkeit | Heeb |publisher=Heebmagazine.com |accessdate=April 24, 2012}} Pekar said that for the first few years of his life, he didn't have friends.''Cleveland'' by Harvey Pekar, illustrated by Joseph Remnant, Zip Comics and Top Shelf Productions, 2012, page 42. The neighborhood he lived in had once been all white but [[White flight|became mostly black by the 1940s]]; as one of the only white kids still living there Pekar was often beaten up. He later believed this instilled in him "a profound sense of inferiority.""{{cite news | url =https://www.nytimes.com/2010/07/13/arts/design/13pekar.html | title = Harvey Pekar, 'American Splendor' Creator, Dies at 70 | first= William | last = Grimes | work = [[The New York Times]] | date = July 12, 2010}} However, this experience also taught him to eventually become a "respected street scrapper." Harvey Pekar graduated from [[Shaker Heights High School]] in 1957, then attended [[Case Western Reserve University]], where he dropped out after a year. He then served in the [[United States Navy]], and after discharge returned to Cleveland where he worked odd jobs before being hired as file [[clerk (position)|clerk]] at Cleveland's Veteran's Administration Hospital. He held this job even after becoming famous, refusing all promotions until he finally retired in 2001. Pekar was married from 1960 to 1972 to his first wife, Karen Delaney.Rhode, Michael G., editor. ''Harvey Pekar: Conversations'' ( Conversations with Comic Artists Series) (University Press of Mississippi, 2008), pp. xiii-xiv. His second wife was Helen Lark Hall.{{citation needed|date=September 2013}} Pekar's third wife was writer [[Joyce Brabner]], with whom he collaborated on ''[[Our Cancer Year]]'', a [[graphic novel]] autobiography of his harrowing yet successful treatment for [[lymphoma]]. He lived in [[Cleveland Heights]], Ohio with Brabner and their foster daughter Danielle Batone.{{cite web|url=http://blog.cleveland.com/metro/2010/07/cleveland_comic-book_legend_ha.html|title=Harvey Pekar, Cleveland comic-book legend, dies at age 70|author=Connors, Joanna|work=[[The Plain Dealer]]|publisher=Cleveland.com|date=July 12, 2010}}{{cite web|work=[[NPR]]|title=Harvey Pekar Dies; Authored 'American Splendor'|first=Neda|authorlink=Neda Ulaby|last=Ulaby|date=July 12, 2010|url=https://www.npr.org/templates/story/story.php?storyId=128465797}} ==Career== ===''American Splendor''=== Pekar's friendship with [[Robert Crumb]] eventually led to the creation of the self-published, autobiographical comic book series ''[[American Splendor]]''. Crumb and Pekar became friends through their mutual love of [[jazz]] records[http://www.wksu.org/features/harveypekar/ "Who is Harvey Pekar?"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060711121347/http://www.wksu.org/features/harveypekar/ |date=July 11, 2006 }}, WKSU.org when Crumb was living in Cleveland in the mid-1960s. Crumb's work in underground comics led Pekar to see the form's possibilities, saying, "Comics could do anything that film could do. And I wanted in on it."[http://www.momocollege.com/article/harvey_pekar Momo College]{{dead link|date=November 2017 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} It took Pekar a decade to do so: "I theorized for maybe ten years about doing comics."[http://metajam.mobi/cinema-actor/-/-/Harvey+Pekar/e+harvey_pekar "Harvey Pekar"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120301200612/http://metajam.mobi/cinema-actor/-/-/Harvey+Pekar/e+harvey_pekar |date=March 1, 2012 }}, Metajam.mobi Around 1972, Pekar laid out some stories with crude stick figures and showed them to Crumb and another artist, [[Robert Armstrong (comics)|Robert Armstrong]]. Impressed, they both offered to illustrate. Pekar & Crumb's one-pager "Crazy Ed" was published as the back cover of Crumb's ''The People's Comics'' (Golden Gate Publishing Company, 1972), becoming Pekar's first published work of comics. Including "Crazy Ed" and before the publication of ''American Splendor'' #1, Pekar wrote a number of other comic stories that were published in a variety of outlets: * "Crazy Ed", with [[Robert Crumb]], in ''The People's Comics'' (Golden Gate Publishing Company, 1972) * "A Mexican Tale," with [[Greg Budgett]] and Munan, in ''Flaming Baloney X'' (Propaganda Ink, c. 1975) * "It Pays to Advertise" with [[Willy Murphy]], in ''[[Flamed-out Funnies]]'' #1 (Rip Off Press, Aug. 1975) * "Ain' It the Truth" with Willy Murphy, in ''Flamed-out Funnies'' #1 (Rip Off Press, Aug. 1975) * "The Boys on the Corner: A Good Shit Is Best" with Willy Murphy, in ''Flamed-out Funnies'' #1 (Rip Off Press, Aug. 1975) * "The Kinsman Cowboys: How'd Ya Get Inta This Bizness Ennyway?" with [[Greg Budgett]] & [[Gary Dumm]], in ''[[Bizarre Sex]]'' #4 (Kitchen Sink Press, Oct. 1975) * "Famous Street Fights: The Champ" with [[Robert Armstrong (comics)|Robert Armstrong]] in ''[[Comix Book]]'' #4 (Kitchen Sink Press, Feb. 1976) * "Don't Rain on My Parade" with Robert Armstrong in ''[[Snarf (comics)|Snarf]]'' #6 (Kitchen Sink Press, Feb. 1976) The first issue of Pekar's self-published ''American Splendor'' series appeared in May 1976, with stories illustrated by the likes of Crumb, Dumm, Budgett, and [[Brian Bram]]. ''American Splendor'' documented Pekar's daily life in the aging neighborhoods of his native Cleveland. Pekar's best-known and longest-running collaborators include Crumb, Dumm, Budgett, [[Spain Rodriguez]], [[Joe Zabel]], [[Gerry Shamray]], [[Frank Stack]], Mark Zingarelli, and [[Joe Sacco]]. In the 2000s, he teamed regularly with artists [[Dean Haspiel]] and [[Josh Neufeld]]. Other cartoonists who worked with him include [[Jim Woodring]], [[Chester Brown]], [[Alison Bechdel]], [[Gilbert Hernandez]], [[Eddie Campbell]], [[David Collier (cartoonist)|David Collier]], [[Drew Friedman (cartoonist)|Drew Friedman]], [[Ho Che Anderson]], [[Rick Geary]], [[Ed Piskor]], [[Hunt Emerson]], [[Bob Fingerman]], [[Brian Bram]], and Alex Wald; as well as such non-traditional illustrators as Pekar's wife, [[Joyce Brabner]], and comics writer [[Alan Moore]]. Stories from the ''American Splendor'' comics have been collected in many books and anthologies. ===''American Splendor'' film=== A [[American Splendor (film)|film adaptation of ''American Splendor'']] was released in 2003, directed by [[Robert Pulcini]] and [[Shari Springer Berman]].[http://www.imdb.com/title/tt0305206/ IMDB Movie Page]. Retrieved December 28, 2008. It featured [[Paul Giamatti]] as Pekar, as well as appearances by Pekar himself. Pekar wrote about the effects of the film in ''American Splendor: Our Movie Year''. In 2006, Pekar released a four-issue ''American Splendor'' miniseries through the [[DC Comics]] [[imprint (trade name)|imprint]] [[Vertigo (comics)|Vertigo]].{{Cite book | last = Irvine | first = Alex | author-link = Alexander C. Irvine | contribution = American Splendor | editor-last = Dougall | editor-first = Alastair | title = The Vertigo Encyclopedia | page = 21 | publisher = [[Dorling Kindersley]] | place = New York | year = 2008 | isbn = 0-7566-4122-5 | oclc = 213309015 | postscript = }} This was collected in the ''American Splendor: Another Day'' paperback. In 2008 Vertigo released a second "season" of ''American Splendor'' that was collected in the ''American Splendor: Another Dollar'' paperback. In addition to his autobiographical work on ''American Splendor'', Pekar wrote a number of biographies. The first of these, ''American Splendor: Unsung Hero'' (2003), documented the [[Vietnam War]] experience of Robert McNeill, one of Pekar's African-American coworkers at Cleveland's [[Veteran's Administration|VA]] hospital. ===Other comics work=== [[File:Harvey Pekar.jpg|thumb|Harvey Pekar at WonderCon 2005, San Francisco]] On October 5, 2005, the [[DC Comics]] imprint [[Vertigo Comics|Vertigo]] released Pekar's autobiographical hardcover ''The Quitter'', with artwork by [[Dean Haspiel]]. The book detailed Pekar's early years. In 2006, Pekar released another biography for [[Ballantine Books|Ballantine]]/[[Random House]], ''Ego & Hubris: The Michael Malice Story'', about the life of [[Michael Malice]], who was the founding editor of ''OverheardinNewYork.com''.{{cite web|url=http://www.overheardinnewyork.com |title=The Voice of the City |publisher=Overheard in New York |accessdate=April 24, 2012}} Pekar was the first guest editor for the collection ''[[The Best American Comics]] 2006'' published by [[Houghton Mifflin]], the first comics collection in the "[[Best American series]]" series. In June 2007, Pekar collaborated with student Heather Roberson and artist [[Ed Piskor]] on the book ''[[Macedonia (comics)|Macedonia]]'', which centers around Roberson's studies in the [[Republic of Macedonia|country]].{{cite web|url=https://shopping.yahoo.com/p:Macedonia:3004941646;_ylc=X3oDMTB1c21tcDhkBF9TAzk2NjMyOTA3BHNlYwNmZWVkBHNsawNib29rcw-- |title=Macedonia – Yahoo! Shopping |publisher=Shopping.yahoo.com |accessdate=April 24, 2012}}{{cite web|url=http://www.sequart.com/columns/?column=1210 |title=Sequart Research & Literacy Organization Columns – High-Low #15: Pekar, Piskor and a Preview of Macedonia |publisher=Sequart.com |accessdate=April 24, 2012}} January 2008 saw another biographical work from Pekar, ''Students for a Democratic Society: A Graphic History'', released through [[Farrar, Straus and Giroux#Current imprints|Hill & Wang]]. In March 2009, Pekar released ''The Beats'', a history of the [[Beat Generation]], including [[Jack Kerouac]] and [[Allen Ginsberg]], illustrated by [[Ed Piskor]].[http://pwbeat.publishersweekly.com/blog/2006/07/13/novel-graphics-looks-at-hoover-beats-genetics "Novel Graphics looks at Hoover, Beats, Genetics"]{{dead link|date=November 2017 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} San Diego Comicon International v2, July 13, 2006. Retrieved July 10, 2008. In May 2009 he released ''Studs Terkel's Working: A Graphic Adaptation''. In 2010, Pekar launched a [[webcomic]] with the online magazine ''[[Smith Magazine|Smith]]'', titled ''The Pekar Project''.{{cite web|url=http://www.smithmag.net/pekarproject |title=The Pekar Project |publisher=Smithmag.net |accessdate=July 12, 2010}} In 2011, Abrams Comicarts published "Yiddishkeit," co-edited by Pekar with [[Paul Buhle]] and with Hershl Hartman, depicting many aspects of Yiddish language and culture. Artists in this anthology include many of Pekar's previous collaborators. ==Theater, music and media appearances== Pekar's comic book success led to a guest appearance on ''[[Late Night with David Letterman]]'' on October 15, 1986. Pekar was invited back repeatedly and made five more appearances in quick succession. These appearances were notable for verbal altercations between Pekar and Letterman, particularly on the subject of General Electric's ownership of NBC. The most heated of these was in the August 31, 1988, episode of ''Late Night'', in which Pekar accused Letterman of appearing to be a [[shill]] for General Electric and Letterman promised never to invite Pekar back on the show.Hynes, James. [http://inthesetimes.com/article/109/the_big_shill/ "The Big Shill,"] ''In These Times'' (SEPTEMBER 21, 1988). However, Pekar did appear on ''Late Night'' again on April 20, 1993, and appeared on the ''[[Late Show With David Letterman]]'' in 1994.{{cite web|website=cleveland.com|title = David Letterman brought Harvey Pekar, his Cleveland cool and a big blow-up to 'Late Night'|url = http://www.cleveland.com/entertainment/index.ssf/2015/05/david_letterman_brought_harvey.html}} Pekar was a prolific [[record collecting|record collector]] as well as a freelance book and jazz critic, focusing on significant figures from jazz's golden age but also championing out-of-mainstream artists such as Birth, [[Scott Fields]], [[Fred Frith]] and [[Joe Maneri]]. He reviewed literary fiction in the early 1990s in such periodicals as the ''Los Angeles Reader'',{{citation needed|date=July 2015}} the ''Review of Contemporary Fiction'',{{citation needed|date=July 2015}} and ''Woodward Review.''{{citation needed|date=July 2015}} Pekar won awards for his essays broadcast on [[Public broadcasting|public radio]]. He appeared in [[Alan Zweig]]'s 2000 documentary film about record collecting, ''[[Vinyl (2000 film)|Vinyl]]''.{{cite web|title=SHOOTING MYSELF IN THE MIRROR: The Obsessive Cinema of Alan Zweig|work=[[Winnipeg Film Group]]|url=http://www.winnipegfilmgroup.com/cinematheque/shooting_myself_in_the_mirror_the_obsessive_cinema_of_alan_zweig.aspx|accessdate=February 12, 2011|deadurl=yes|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20110207230141/http://www.winnipegfilmgroup.com/cinematheque/shooting_myself_in_the_mirror_the_obsessive_cinema_of_alan_zweig.aspx|archivedate=February 7, 2011|df=mdy-all}} In August 2007, Pekar was featured on the Cleveland episode of ''[[Anthony Bourdain: No Reservations]]'' with host [[Anthony Bourdain]].{{cite web|url=http://potrzebie.blogspot.com/2007/08/celeb-chef-anthony-bourdain-meets_18.html |title=Harvey Pekar Meets Anthony Bourdain |publisher=Potrzebie.blogspot.com |date=August 18, 2007 |accessdate=April 24, 2012}} While ''American Splendor'' theater adaptations had previously occurred,{{cite web|author=Kistler, Alan |url=http://www.comicsalliance.com/2010/07/13/harvey-pekar-a-timeline-of-a-comic-book-icon/ |title=Harvey Pekar: A Timeline of a Comic Book Icon – ComicsAlliance | Comic book culture, news, humor, commentary, and reviews |publisher=ComicsAlliance |date=July 13, 2010 |accessdate=April 24, 2012 |deadurl=yes |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20120514052147/http://www.comicsalliance.com/2010/07/13/harvey-pekar-a-timeline-of-a-comic-book-icon/ |archivedate=May 14, 2012 |df=mdy-all }} in 2009, Pekar made his theatrical debut with ''Leave Me Alone!'', a [[jazz]] opera for which Pekar wrote the [[libretto]]. ''Leave Me Alone!'' featured music by [[Dan Plonsey]] and was co-produced by [[Real Time Opera]] and [[Oberlin College]], premiering at [[Finney Chapel]] on January 31, 2009.{{cite web|url=https://www.npr.org/templates/story/story.php?storyId=100031337 |title=NPR: Harvey Pekar Makes His Opera Debut |publisher=NPR.org |accessdate=April 16, 2014}} In 2009, Pekar was featured in ''[[The Cartoonist]],'' a documentary film on the life and work of [[Jeff Smith (cartoonist)|Jeff Smith]], creator of ''[[Bone (comics)|Bone]].''{{cite web|url=http://www.thecartoonistmovie.com |title=The Cartoonist: Jeff Smith, Bone and the Changing Face of Comics |publisher=Thecartoonistmovie.com |accessdate=July 12, 2010}} ==Death and work released posthumously== Shortly before 1 a.m. on July 12, 2010, Pekar's wife found Pekar dead in their [[Cleveland Heights]], Ohio, home.{{cite news | last = Connors | first= Joanna | url = http://blog.cleveland.com/metro/2010/07/cleveland_comic-book_legend_ha.html | title = Cleveland Comic-Book Legend Harvey Pekar Dead at Age 70 | work = [[The Plain Dealer]] | location =[[Cleveland, Ohio]] | date = July 12, 2010 | quote= He was recently diagnosed with prostate cancer, and also suffered high blood pressure, asthma and clinical depression, which fueled his art but often made his life painful.|archiveurl = http://arquivo.pt/wayback/20100804232837/http://blog.cleveland.com/metro/2010/07/cleveland_comic-book_legend_ha.html | archivedate=August 4, 2010|deadurl=no}} No immediate cause was determined,{{cite news |first=William | last = Grimes |title=Harvey Pekar, ‘American Splendor’ Creator, Dies at 70 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2010/07/13/arts/design/13pekar.html?ref=harvey_pekar |quote=A spokesman for the Cuyahoga County coroner’s office said that no cause of death had yet been determined. Capt. Michael Cannon of the Cleveland Heights Police Department, which was summoned to Mr. Pekar's home by his wife, Joyce Brabner, told The Associated Press that Mr. Pekar had suffered from prostate cancer, asthma, high blood pressure and depression. |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=July 12, 2010 |accessdate=September 2, 2010 |authorlink= William Grimes (author) }} but in October the [[Cuyahoga County]] coroner's office ruled it was an accidental overdose of [[antidepressant]]s [[fluoxetine]] and [[bupropion]].{{cite web |url=http://blog.cleveland.com/metro/2010/10/coroner_rules_that_harvey_peka.html |title=Coroner rules that Harvey Pekar's death due to 'natural causes' |last=Galbinca |first=Pat |work=The Plain Dealer | location =Cleveland, Ohio | date=October 20, 2010 |accessdate=October 20, 2010}} Pekar had been diagnosed with cancer for the third time and was about to undergo treatment. His headstone features one of his quotations as an epitaph: "Life is about women, gigs, an' bein' creative."[http://www.findagrave.com/cgi-bin/fg.cgi?page=pv&GRid=54845318&PIpi=68182522 Findagrave.com: Harvey Lawrence Pekar] Some Pekar works were to be released posthumously,{{cite news| url=https://www.nytimes.com/2010/09/05/arts/design/05pekar.html?_r=1&pagewanted=2&bl | work=The New York Times | first=Dave | last=Itzkoff | title=The Unsettled Afterlife of Harvey Pekar | date=September 1, 2010}} including two collaborations with Joyce Brabner, ''The Big Book Of Marriage'' and ''Harvey and Joyce Plumb the Depths of Depression'', as well as a collection of the webcomics that ran as a part of ''The Pekar Project''.{{cite web| url= http://www.comicbookresources.com/?page=article&id=28968| title= NYCC: Remembering Harvey Pekar| date= October 19, 2010| first= Alex| last= Dueben| publisher= [[Comic Book Resources]]| accessdate= 2014-01-09| archivedate= January 9, 2014| archiveurl= https://www.webcitation.org/6MVI6VuKL?url=http://www.comicbookresources.com/?page=article&id=28968| deadurl= no| df= mdy-all}} Archive version requires blocking-off text in order to make black-on-black text visible. Working with illustrator [[Summer McClinton]], Pekar also finished a book on American Marxist Louis Proyect, tentatively called ''The Unrepentant Marxist'', after Proyect's blog. In the works since 2008, the book was to be published by Random House. After a conflict between Proyect and Joyce Brabner, Brabner announced that she would hold the book back indefinitely.{{cite web |url=http://louisproyect.org/category/pekar/ |title=Articles tagged 'Pekar' on Louis Proyect's blog, Unrepentant Marxist |website=Unrepentant Marxist |accessdate=2014-04-07}} As of April 2014, those four titles have not been released. In December 2010, the last story Pekar wrote — "Harvey Pekar Meets the Thing", in which Pekar has a conversation with [[The Thing (comics)|Ben Grimm]] — was published in the [[Marvel Comics]] anthology ''[[Strange Tales|Strange Tales II]]''; the story was illustrated by [[Ty Templeton]].[http://goodcomics.comicbookresources.com/2010/12/17/what-i-bought-15-december-2010/ What I Bought (15 December 2010)], by Greg Burgas, at [[Comic Book Resources]]; published 17 December 2010; retrieved 25 June 2014 ==Legacy== {| class="toccolours" style="float: right; margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 1em; font-size: 85%; background:#c6dbf7; color:black; width:23em; max-width: 25%;" cellspacing="5" | style="text-align: left;" | "I think probably the most important thing about ''American Splendor'', in all its incarnations, is that there were very few people in the earlier days of comics prepared to put their work where their mouth was. Harvey believed there was no limit to how good comics could be. To chronicle his life from these tiny wonderful moments of magic and of heartbreak — and the most important thing was that he did it." |- | style="text-align: left;" | —[[Neil Gaiman]] |} Frequently described as the "poet laureate of Cleveland," Pekar "helped change the appreciation for, and perceptions of, the graphic novel, the drawn memoir, the autobiographical comic narrative." His ''American Splendor'' "remains one of the most compelling and transformative series in the history of comics.""[http://latimesblogs.latimes.com/jacketcopy/2012/07/the-reading-life-harvey-pekars-jewish-question.html The Reading Life: Harvey Pekar's Jewish question]" by David L. Ulin, Jacket Copy, The LA Times, July 12, 2012. In addition, Pekar was the first author to publicly distribute "memoir comic books.""[http://www.jewishbookcouncil.org/_blog/The_ProsenPeople/post/Graphic_Memoir_The_Legacy_of_Harvey_Pekar/ Graphic Memoir: The Legacy of Harvey Pekar]" by JT Waldman, The Prosen People, The Jewish Book Council, July 3, 2012. While it is common today for people to publicly write about their lives on blogs, social media platforms, and in graphic novels, "In the mid-seventies, Harvey Pekar was doing all this before it was ubiquitous and commercialized." In October 2012 a statue of Pekar was installed at the [[Cleveland Heights]]-University Heights Library, a place he visited almost daily.[http://www.kickstarter.com/projects/1844705603/harvey-pekar-library-statue-comics-as-art-and-lite]"[http://www.cleveland.com/metro/index.ssf/2012/10/statue_of_harvey_pekar_unveile.html Harvey Pekar statue unveiled at library is tribute to the late graphic novelist from Cleveland]" by Tom Breckenridge, The Plain Dealer, October 14, 2012. ==Awards== * 1987: [[American Book Award]] for the first ''American Splendor'' anthology * 1995: [[Harvey Award]] Best Graphic Album of Original Work (for ''Our Cancer Year''){{cite web|url=http://www.harveyawards.org/awards_1995win.html |title=The Harvey Awards |publisher=The Harvey Awards |accessdate=July 12, 2010 |deadurl=yes |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20100716172409/http://www.harveyawards.org/awards_1995win.html |archivedate=July 16, 2010 |df=mdy-all }} ==Bibliography== [[File:HPekar.jpg|thumbnail|right| Harvey Pekar and Joyce Brabner at Hallwalls, Buffalo, New York (October 4, 1985)]] * ''American Splendor: The Life and Times of Harvey Pekar'' (Doubleday, 1986) * ''More American Splendor'' (Doubleday, 1987) {{ISBN|0-385-24073-2}} * ''The New American Splendor Anthology'' ([[Four Walls Eight Windows]], 1991) {{ISBN|0-941423-64-6}} * ''[[Our Cancer Year]]'', with Joyce Brabner and Frank Stack (Four Walls Eight Windows, 1994) {{ISBN|1-56858-011-8}} * ''American Splendor Presents: Bob & Harv's Comics'', with R. [[Joyce Brabner]] (1984-2010; his death; 1 foster child) | children = Danielle Batone }} '''Harvey Lawrence Pekar''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|p|iː|k|ɑr}}; October 8, 1939 – July 12, 2010) was an American [[Underground comics|underground comic book]] writer, music critic, and media personality, best known for his autobiographical ''[[American Splendor]]'' comic series. In 2003, the series inspired a well-received [[American Splendor (film)|film adaptation]] of the same name. Frequently described as the "poet laureate of Cleveland,"{{cite web|url=http://blog.travelchannel.com/anthony-bourdain/read/the-original-goodbye-splendor/|title=The Original (Goodbye Splendor)|author=Bourdain, Anthony|authorlink=Anthony Bourdain|publisher=[[Travel Channel]]|date=July 13, 2010}}"[http://www.tabletmag.com/scroll/39242/harvey-pekar-dies Harvey Pekar Dies: Comic book writer was 'poet laureate of Cleveland']" by Marc Tracy, Tablet, July 12, 2010 Pekar "helped change the appreciation for, and perceptions of, the graphic novel, the drawn memoir, the autobiographical comic narrative.""[https://www.washingtonpost.com/blogs/comic-riffs/post/harvey-pekar-remembering-the-man--and-legacy--one-year-later/2011/07/13/gIQAbqodCI_blog.html HARVEY PEKAR: Remembering the man — and legacy — one year later]" by Michael Cavna, The Washington Post, 7/13/2011 Pekar described his work as "autobiography written as it's happening. The theme is about staying alive, getting a job, finding a mate, having a place to live, finding a creative outlet. Life is a [[attrition warfare|war of attrition]]. You have to stay active on all fronts. It's one thing after another. I've tried to control a chaotic universe. And it's a losing battle. But I can't let go. I've tried, but I can't."[http://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/obituaries/culture-obituaries/books-obituaries/7888494/Harvey-Pekar.html "Harvey Pekar"] (obituary), ''[[The Daily Telegraph]]'', July 13, 2010 ==Life== Harvey Pekar and his younger brother Allen were born in [[Cleveland]], Ohio to Saul and Dora Pekar, immigrants from [[Białystok]], Poland. Saul Pekar was a [[Talmud]]ic scholar who owned a grocery store on Kinsman Avenue, with the family living above the store. While Pekar said he wasn't close to his parents due to their dissimilar backgrounds and because they worked all the time, he still "marveled at how devoted they were to each other. They had so much love and admiration for one another."{{cite book | title = Cleveland | first= Harvey | last= Pekar | first2= Joseph (illustrations) | last2= Remnant | publisher = Zip Comics and Top Shelf Productions | year= 2012 | page= 53}} As a child, Pekar's first language was [[Yiddish]], and he learned to read and appreciate novels in the language.{{cite web|url=http://heebmagazine.com/harvey-pekars-yiddishkeit-exclusive-art-and-comix/34706 |title=Exclusive: A Smorgasbord of Art and Comics Celebrating Harvey Pekar’s Yiddishkeit | Heeb |publisher=Heebmagazine.com |accessdate=April 24, 2012}} Pekar said that for the first few years of his life, he didn't have friends.''Cleveland'' by Harvey Pekar, illustrated by Joseph Remnant, Zip Comics and Top Shelf Productions, 2012, page 42. The neighborhood he lived in had once been all white but [[White flight|became mostly black by the 1940s]]; as one of the only white kids still living there Pekar was often beaten up. He later believed this instilled in him "a profound sense of inferiority.""{{cite news | url =https://www.nytimes.com/2010/07/13/arts/design/13pekar.html | title = Harvey Pekar, 'American Splendor' Creator, Dies at 70 | first= William | last = Grimes | work = [[The New York Times]] | date = July 12, 2010}} However, this experience also taught him to eventually become a "respected street scrapper." Harvey Pekar graduated from [[Shaker Heights High School]] in 1957, then attended [[Case Western Reserve University]], where he dropped out after a year. He then served in the [[United States Navy]], and after discharge returned to Cleveland where he worked odd jobs before being hired as file [[clerk (position)|clerk]] at Cleveland's Veteran's Administration Hospital. He held this job even after becoming famous, refusing all promotions until he finally retired in 2001. Pekar was married from 1960 to 1972 to his first wife, Karen Delaney.{{citation needed|date=September 2013}} His second wife was Helen Lark Hall.{{citation needed|date=September 2013}} Pekar's third wife was writer [[Joyce Brabner]],{{citation needed|date=September 2013}} with whom he collaborated on ''[[Our Cancer Year]]'', a [[graphic novel]] autobiography of his harrowing yet successful treatment for [[lymphoma]]. He lived in [[Cleveland Heights]], Ohio with Brabner and their foster daughter Danielle Batone.{{cite web|url=http://blog.cleveland.com/metro/2010/07/cleveland_comic-book_legend_ha.html|title=Harvey Pekar, Cleveland comic-book legend, dies at age 70|author=Connors, Joanna|work=[[The Plain Dealer]]|publisher=Cleveland.com|date=July 12, 2010}}{{cite web|work=[[NPR]]|title=Harvey Pekar Dies; Authored 'American Splendor'|first=Neda|authorlink=Neda Ulaby|last=Ulaby|date=July 12, 2010|url=http://www.npr.org/templates/story/story.php?storyId=128465797}} ==Career== ===''American Splendor''=== Pekar's friendship with [[Robert Crumb]] eventually led to the creation of the self-published, autobiographical comic book series ''[[American Splendor]]''. Crumb and Pekar became friends through their mutual love of [[jazz]] records[http://www.wksu.org/features/harveypekar/ "Who is Harvey Pekar?"], WKSU.org when Crumb was living in Cleveland in the mid-1960s. Crumb's work in underground comics led Pekar to see the form's possibilities, saying, "Comics could do anything that film could do. And I wanted in on it."[http://www.momocollege.com/article/harvey_pekar Momo College] It took Pekar a decade to do so: "I theorized for maybe ten years about doing comics."[http://metajam.mobi/cinema-actor/-/-/Harvey+Pekar/e+harvey_pekar "Harvey Pekar"], Metajam.mobi Around 1972, Pekar laid out some stories with crude stick figures and showed them to Crumb and another artist, [[Robert Armstrong (comics)|Robert Armstrong]]. Impressed, they both offered to illustrate. Pekar & Crumb's one-pager "Crazy Ed" was published as the back cover of Crumb's ''The People's Comics'' (Golden Gate Publishing Company, 1972), becoming Pekar's first published work of comics. Including "Crazy Ed" and before the publication of ''American Splendor'' #1, Pekar wrote a number of other comic stories that were published in a variety of outlets: * "Crazy Ed", with [[Robert Crumb]], in ''The People's Comics'' (Golden Gate Publishing Company, 1972) * "A Mexican Tale," with [[Greg Budgett]] and Munan, in ''Flaming Baloney X'' (Propaganda Ink, c. 1975) * "It Pays to Advertise" with [[Willy Murphy]], in ''[[Flamed-out Funnies]]'' #1 (Rip Off Press, Aug. 1975) * "Ain' It the Truth" with Willy Murphy, in ''Flamed-out Funnies'' #1 (Rip Off Press, Aug. 1975) * "The Boys on the Corner: A Good Shit Is Best" with Willy Murphy, in ''Flamed-out Funnies'' #1 (Rip Off Press, Aug. 1975) * "The Kinsman Cowboys: How'd Ya Get Inta This Bizness Ennyway?" with [[Greg Budgett]] & [[Gary Dumm]], in ''[[Bizarre Sex]]'' #4 (Kitchen Sink Press, Oct. 1975) * "Famous Street Fights: The Champ" with [[Robert Armstrong (comics)|Robert Armstrong]] in ''[[Comix Book]]'' #4 (Kitchen Sink Press, Feb. 1976) * "Don't Rain on My Parade" with Robert Armstrong in ''[[Snarf (comics)|Snarf]]'' #6 (Kitchen Sink Press, Feb. 1976) The first issue of Pekar's self-published ''American Splendor'' series appeared in May 1976, with stories illustrated by the likes of Crumb, Dumm, Budgett, and [[Brian Bram]]. ''American Splendor'' documented Pekar's daily life in the aging neighborhoods of his native Cleveland. Pekar's best-known and longest-running collaborators include Crumb, Dumm, Budgett, [[Spain Rodriguez]], [[Joe Zabel]], [[Gerry Shamray]], [[Frank Stack]], Mark Zingarelli, and [[Joe Sacco]]. In the 2000s, he teamed regularly with artists [[Dean Haspiel]] and [[Josh Neufeld]]. Other cartoonists who worked with him include [[Jim Woodring]], [[Chester Brown]], [[Alison Bechdel]], [[Gilbert Hernandez]], [[Eddie Campbell]], [[David Collier (cartoonist)|David Collier]], [[Drew Friedman (cartoonist)|Drew Friedman]], [[Ho Che Anderson]], [[Rick Geary]], [[Ed Piskor]], [[Hunt Emerson]], [[Bob Fingerman]], [[Brian Bram]], and Alex Wald; as well as such non-traditional illustrators as Pekar's wife, [[Joyce Brabner]], and comics writer [[Alan Moore]]. Stories from the ''American Splendor'' comics have been collected in many books and anthologies. ===''American Splendor'' film=== A [[American Splendor (film)|film adaptation of ''American Splendor'']] was released in 2003, directed by [[Robert Pulcini]] and [[Shari Springer Berman]].[http://www.imdb.com/title/tt0305206/ IMDB Movie Page]. Retrieved December 28, 2008. It featured [[Paul Giamatti]] as Pekar, as well as appearances by Pekar himself. Pekar wrote about the effects of the film in ''American Splendor: Our Movie Year''. In 2006, Pekar released a four-issue ''American Splendor'' miniseries through the [[DC Comics]] [[imprint (trade name)|imprint]] [[Vertigo (comics)|Vertigo]].{{Cite book | last = Irvine | first = Alex | author-link = Alexander C. Irvine | contribution = American Splendor | editor-last = Dougall | editor-first = Alastair | title = The Vertigo Encyclopedia | page = 21 | publisher = [[Dorling Kindersley]] | place = New York | year = 2008 | isbn = 0-7566-4122-5 | oclc = 213309015 | postscript = }} This was collected in the ''American Splendor: Another Day'' paperback. In 2008 Vertigo released a second "season" of ''American Splendor'' that was collected in the ''American Splendor: Another Dollar'' paperback. In addition to his autobiographical work on ''American Splendor'', Pekar wrote a number of biographies. The first of these, ''American Splendor: Unsung Hero'' (2003), documented the [[Vietnam War]] experience of Robert McNeill, one of Pekar's African-American coworkers at Cleveland's [[Veteran's Administration|VA]] hospital. ===Other comics work=== [[File:Harvey Pekar.jpg|thumb|Harvey Pekar at WonderCon 2005, San Francisco]] On October 5, 2005, the [[DC Comics]] imprint [[Vertigo Comics|Vertigo]] released Pekar's autobiographical hardcover ''The Quitter'', with artwork by [[Dean Haspiel]]. The book detailed Pekar's early years. In 2006, Pekar released another biography for [[Ballantine Books|Ballantine]]/[[Random House]], ''Ego & Hubris: The Michael Malice Story'', about the life of [[Michael Malice]], who was the founding editor of ''OverheardinNewYork.com''.{{cite web|url=http://www.overheardinnewyork.com |title=The Voice of the City |publisher=Overheard in New York |accessdate=April 24, 2012}} Pekar was the first guest editor for the collection ''[[The Best American Comics]] 2006'' published by [[Houghton Mifflin]], the first comics collection in the "[[Best American series]]" series. In June 2007, Pekar collaborated with student Heather Roberson and artist [[Ed Piskor]] on the book ''[[Macedonia (comics)|Macedonia]]'', which centers around Roberson's studies in the [[Republic of Macedonia|country]].{{cite web|url=https://shopping.yahoo.com/p:Macedonia:3004941646;_ylc=X3oDMTB1c21tcDhkBF9TAzk2NjMyOTA3BHNlYwNmZWVkBHNsawNib29rcw-- |title=Macedonia – Yahoo! Shopping |publisher=Shopping.yahoo.com |accessdate=April 24, 2012}}{{cite web|url=http://www.sequart.com/columns/?column=1210 |title=Sequart Research & Literacy Organization Columns – High-Low #15: Pekar, Piskor and a Preview of Macedonia |publisher=Sequart.com |accessdate=April 24, 2012}} January 2008 saw another biographical work from Pekar, ''Students for a Democratic Society: A Graphic History'', released through [[Farrar, Straus and Giroux#Current imprints|Hill & Wang]]. In March 2009, Pekar released ''The Beats'', a history of the [[Beat Generation]], including [[Jack Kerouac]] and [[Allen Ginsberg]], illustrated by [[Ed Piskor]].[http://pwbeat.publishersweekly.com/blog/2006/07/13/novel-graphics-looks-at-hoover-beats-genetics "Novel Graphics looks at Hoover, Beats, Genetics"] San Diego Comicon International v2, July 13, 2006. Retrieved July 10, 2008. In May 2009 he released ''Studs Terkel's Working: A Graphic Adaptation''. In 2010, Pekar launched a [[webcomic]] with the online magazine ''[[Smith Magazine|Smith]]'', titled ''The Pekar Project''.{{cite web|url=http://www.smithmag.net/pekarproject |title=The Pekar Project |publisher=Smithmag.net |accessdate=July 12, 2010}} In 2011, Abrams Comicarts published "Yiddishkeit," co-edited by Pekar with [[Paul Buhle]] and with Hershl Hartman, depicting many aspects of Yiddish language and culture. Artists in this anthology include many of Pekar's previous collaborators. ==Theater, music and media appearances== Pekar's comic book success led to a guest appearance on ''[[Late Night with David Letterman]]'' on October 15, 1986. Pekar was invited back repeatedly and made five more appearances in quick succession. These appearances were notable for verbal altercations between Pekar and Letterman, particularly on the subject of General Electric's ownership of NBC. The most heated of these was in the August 31, 1988 episode of ''Late Night'', in which Pekar accused Letterman of appearing to be a [[shill]] for General Electric and Letterman promised never to invite Pekar back on the show. However, Pekar did appear on ''Late Night'' again on April 20, 1993, and appeared on the ''[[Late Show With David Letterman]]'' in 1994.{{cite web|website=cleveland.com|title = David Letterman brought Harvey Pekar, his Cleveland cool and a big blow-up to 'Late Night'|url = http://www.cleveland.com/entertainment/index.ssf/2015/05/david_letterman_brought_harvey.html}} Pekar was a prolific [[record collecting|record collector]] as well as a freelance book and jazz critic, focusing on significant figures from jazz's golden age but also championing out-of-mainstream artists such as Birth, [[Scott Fields]], [[Fred Frith]] and [[Joe Maneri]]. He reviewed literary fiction in the early 1990s in such periodicals as the ''Los Angeles Reader'',{{citation needed|date=July 2015}} the ''Review of Contemporary Fiction'',{{citation needed|date=July 2015}} and ''Woodward Review.''{{citation needed|date=July 2015}} Pekar won awards for his essays broadcast on [[Public broadcasting|public radio]]. He appeared in [[Alan Zweig]]'s 2000 documentary film about record collecting, ''[[Vinyl (2000 film)|Vinyl]]''.{{cite web|title=SHOOTING MYSELF IN THE MIRROR: The Obsessive Cinema of Alan Zweig|work=[[Winnipeg Film Group]]|url=http://www.winnipegfilmgroup.com/cinematheque/shooting_myself_in_the_mirror_the_obsessive_cinema_of_alan_zweig.aspx|accessdate=February 12, 2011}} In August 2007, Pekar was featured on the Cleveland episode of ''[[Anthony Bourdain: No Reservations]]'' with host [[Anthony Bourdain]].{{cite web|url=http://potrzebie.blogspot.com/2007/08/celeb-chef-anthony-bourdain-meets_18.html |title=Harvey Pekar Meets Anthony Bourdain |publisher=Potrzebie.blogspot.com |date=August 18, 2007 |accessdate=April 24, 2012}} While ''American Splendor'' theater adaptations had previously occurred,{{cite web|author=Kistler, Alan |url=http://www.comicsalliance.com/2010/07/13/harvey-pekar-a-timeline-of-a-comic-book-icon/ |title=Harvey Pekar: A Timeline of a Comic Book Icon – ComicsAlliance | Comic book culture, news, humor, commentary, and reviews |publisher=ComicsAlliance |date=July 13, 2010 |accessdate=April 24, 2012 |deadurl=yes |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20120514052147/http://www.comicsalliance.com/2010/07/13/harvey-pekar-a-timeline-of-a-comic-book-icon/ |archivedate=May 14, 2012 |df=mdy-all }} in 2009, Pekar made his theatrical debut with ''Leave Me Alone!'', a [[jazz]] opera for which Pekar wrote the [[libretto]]. ''Leave Me Alone!'' featured music by [[Dan Plonsey]] and was co-produced by [[Real Time Opera]] and [[Oberlin College]] premiering at [[Finney Chapel]] on January 31, 2009.{{cite web|url=http://www.npr.org/templates/story/story.php?storyId=100031337 |title=NPR: Harvey Pekar Makes His Opera Debut |publisher=NPR.org |accessdate=April 16, 2014}} In 2009, Pekar was featured in ''[[The Cartoonist]],'' a documentary film on the life and work of [[Jeff Smith (cartoonist)|Jeff Smith]], creator of ''[[Bone (comics)|Bone]].''{{cite web|url=http://www.thecartoonistmovie.com |title=The Cartoonist: Jeff Smith, Bone and the Changing Face of Comics |publisher=Thecartoonistmovie.com |accessdate=July 12, 2010}} ==Death and work released posthumously== Shortly before 1 a.m. on July 12, 2010, Pekar's wife found Pekar dead in their [[Cleveland Heights]], Ohio, home.{{cite news | last = Connors | first= Joanna | url = http://blog.cleveland.com/metro/2010/07/cleveland_comic-book_legend_ha.html | title = Cleveland Comic-Book Legend Harvey Pekar Dead at Age 70 | work = [[The Plain Dealer]] | location =[[Cleveland, Ohio]] | date = July 12, 2010 | quote= He was recently diagnosed with prostate cancer, and also suffered high blood pressure, asthma and clinical depression, which fueled his art but often made his life painful.|archiveurl = http://arquivo.pt/wayback/20100804232837/http://blog.cleveland.com/metro/2010/07/cleveland_comic-book_legend_ha.html | archivedate=August 4, 2010|deadurl=no}} No immediate cause was determined,{{cite news |first=William | last = Grimes |title=Harvey Pekar, ‘American Splendor’ Creator, Dies at 70 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2010/07/13/arts/design/13pekar.html?ref=harvey_pekar |quote=A spokesman for the Cuyahoga County coroner’s office said that no cause of death had yet been determined. Capt. Michael Cannon of the Cleveland Heights Police Department, which was summoned to Mr. Pekar's home by his wife, Joyce Brabner, told The Associated Press that Mr. Pekar had suffered from prostate cancer, asthma, high blood pressure and depression. |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=July 12, 2010 |accessdate=September 2, 2010 |authorlink= William Grimes (author) }} but in October the [[Cuyahoga County]] coroner's office ruled it was an accidental overdose of [[antidepressant]]s [[fluoxetine]] and [[bupropion]].{{cite web |url=http://blog.cleveland.com/metro/2010/10/coroner_rules_that_harvey_peka.html |title=Coroner rules that Harvey Pekar's death due to 'natural causes' |last=Galbinca |first=Pat |work=The Plain Dealer | location =Cleveland, Ohio | date=October 20, 2010 |accessdate=October 20, 2010}} Pekar had been diagnosed with cancer for the third time and was about to undergo treatment. His headstone features one of his quotations as an epitaph: "Life is about women, gigs, an' bein' creative."[http://www.findagrave.com/cgi-bin/fg.cgi?page=pv&GRid=54845318&PIpi=68182522 Findagrave.com: Harvey Lawrence Pekar] Some Pekar works were to be released posthumously,{{cite news| url=https://www.nytimes.com/2010/09/05/arts/design/05pekar.html?_r=1&pagewanted=2&bl | work=The New York Times | first=Dave | last=Itzkoff | title=The Unsettled Afterlife of Harvey Pekar | date=September 1, 2010}} including two collaborations with Joyce Brabner, ''The Big Book Of Marriage'' and ''Harvey and Joyce Plumb the Depths of Depression'', as well as a collection of the webcomics that ran as a part of ''The Pekar Project''.{{cite web | url = http://www.comicbookresources.com/?page=article&id=28968 | title = NYCC: Remembering Harvey Pekar | date= October 19, 2010| first=Alex | last= Dueben| publisher= [[Comic Book Resources]] | accessdate= 2014-01-09 | archivedate= January 9, 2014 | archiveurl =https://www.webcitation.org/6MVI6VuKL?url=http://www.comicbookresources.com/?page%3Darticle%26id%3D28968 | deadurl= no}} Archive version requires blocking-off text in order to make black-on-black text visible. Working with illustrator [[Summer McClinton]], Pekar also finished a book on American Marxist Louis Proyect, tentatively called ''The Unrepentant Marxist'', after Proyect's blog. In the works since 2008, the book was to be published by Random House. After a conflict between Proyect and Joyce Brabner, Brabner announced that she would hold the book back indefinitely.{{cite web |url=http://louisproyect.org/category/pekar/ |title=Articles tagged 'Pekar' on Louis Proyect's blog, Unrepentant Marxist |website=Unrepentant Marxist |accessdate=2014-04-07}} As of April 2014, those four titles have not been released. In December 2010, the last story Pekar wrote — "Harvey Pekar Meets the Thing", in which Pekar has a conversation with [[The Thing (comics)|Ben Grimm]] — was published in the [[Marvel Comics]] anthology ''[[Strange Tales|Strange Tales II]]''; the story was illustrated by [[Ty Templeton]].[http://goodcomics.comicbookresources.com/2010/12/17/what-i-bought-15-december-2010/ What I Bought (15 December 2010)], by Greg Burgas, at [[Comic Book Resources]]; published 17 December 2010; retrieved 25 June 2014 ==Legacy== {| class="toccolours" style="float: right; margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 1em; font-size: 85%; background:#c6dbf7; color:black; width:23em; max-width: 25%;" cellspacing="5" | style="text-align: left;" | "I think probably the most important thing about ''American Splendor'', in all its incarnations, is that there were very few people in the earlier days of comics prepared to put their work where their mouth was. Harvey believed there was no limit to how good comics could be. To chronicle his life from these tiny wonderful moments of magic and of heartbreak — and the most important thing was that he did it." |- | style="text-align: left;" | —[[Neil Gaiman]] |} Frequently described as the "poet laureate of Cleveland," Pekar "helped change the appreciation for, and perceptions of, the graphic novel, the drawn memoir, the autobiographical comic narrative." His ''American Splendor'' "remains one of the most compelling and transformative series in the history of comics.""[http://latimesblogs.latimes.com/jacketcopy/2012/07/the-reading-life-harvey-pekars-jewish-question.html The Reading Life: Harvey Pekar's Jewish question]" by David L. Ulin, Jacket Copy, The LA Times, July 12, 2012. In addition, Pekar was the first author to publicly distribute "memoir comic books.""[http://www.jewishbookcouncil.org/_blog/The_ProsenPeople/post/Graphic_Memoir_The_Legacy_of_Harvey_Pekar/ Graphic Memoir: The Legacy of Harvey Pekar]" by JT Waldman, The Prosen People, The Jewish Book Council, July 3, 2012. While it is common today for people to publicly write about their lives on blogs, social media platforms, and in graphic novels, "In the mid-seventies, Harvey Pekar was doing all this before it was ubiquitous and commercialized." In October 2012 a statue of Pekar was installed at the [[Cleveland Heights]]-University Heights Library, a place he visited almost daily.[http://www.kickstarter.com/projects/1844705603/harvey-pekar-library-statue-comics-as-art-and-lite]"[http://www.cleveland.com/metro/index.ssf/2012/10/statue_of_harvey_pekar_unveile.html Harvey Pekar statue unveiled at library is tribute to the late graphic novelist from Cleveland]" by Tom Breckenridge, The Plain Dealer, October 14, 2012. ==Awards== * 1987: [[American Book Award]] for the first ''American Splendor'' anthology * 1995: [[Harvey Award]] Best Graphic Album of Original Work (for ''Our Cancer Year''){{cite web|url=http://www.harveyawards.org/awards_1995win.html |title=The Harvey Awards |publisher=The Harvey Awards |accessdate=July 12, 2010 |deadurl=yes |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20100716172409/http://www.harveyawards.org/awards_1995win.html |archivedate=July 16, 2010 |df=mdy-all }} ==Bibliography== [[File:HPekar.jpg|thumbnail|right| Harvey Pekar and Joyce Brabner at Hallwalls, Buffalo, New York (October 4, 1985)]] * ''American Splendor: The Life and Times of Harvey Pekar'' (Doubleday, 1986) * ''More American Splendor'' (Doubleday, 1987) {{ISBN|0-385-24073-2}} * ''The New American Splendor Anthology'' ([[Four Walls Eight Windows]], 1991) {{ISBN|0-941423-64-6}} * ''[[Our Cancer Year]]'', with Joyce Brabner and Frank Stack (Four Walls Eight Windows, 1994) {{ISBN|1-56858-011-8}} * ''American Splendor Presents: Bob & Harv's Comics'', with R. '''Henry W. Bloch School of Management''' (formerly known as '''Henry W. Bloch School of Business and Public Administration''') is an [[Association to Advance Collegiate Schools of Business|AACSB]] accredited [[business school]] founded in 1952 at the [[UMKC|University of Missouri-Kansas City]] in [[Kansas City, Missouri]]. It offers undergraduate and graduate degrees in [[Business]], [[Accounting]] and [[Public Administration]]. It is named after Alumnus [[Henry W. Bloch]], founder of [[H&R Block]].<ref>[http://www.bloch.umkc.edu/about-the-bloch-school/bloch-fast-facts/index.aspx Bloch School Fast Facts]</ref> The Bloch School also offers [[National Association of Schools of Public Affairs and Administration|NASPAA]] accredited degrees in [[Public administration]].

==Rankings==

The school's [[Master of Business Administration|Executive MBA]] was ranked once by ''[[Financial Times]]'' and the [[Master of Public Administration]] (MPA) in Non-Profit Management is ranked among the top 25 of the [[United States]] by ''[[U.S. News & World Report]]''.<ref>[http://www.bloch.umkc.edu/about-the-bloch-school/index.aspx About the Bloch School]</ref> As one of the most entrepreneurial schools in the nation,<ref>NBC Action News [http://www.nbcactionnews.com/dpp/lifestyle/proud_to_call_it_home/umkc's-henry-w-bloch-school-of-business-and-public-administration-receives-national-accolades UMKC's Henry W Bloch School of Business and Public Administration receives national accolades] 14 November 2010</ref>  it was ranked #25 by ''[[The Princeton Review]]'' <ref>Kansas City Business Journal [http://www.bizjournals.com/kansascity/stories/2009/09/21/daily18.html UMKC's Bloch School of Business ranks among top 25 entrepreneurship programs] September 22, 2012</ref>

In 2012, the ''[[Journal of Product Innovation Management]]'' published a study that ranked the school number 1 in the world for research in [[innovation management]].<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1111/j.1540-5885.2011.00898.x |title=Perspective: Ranking of the World's Top Innovation Management Scholars and Universities |journal=Journal of Product Innovation Management |volume=29 |issue=2 |pages=319 |year=2012 |last1=Yang |first1=Pianpian |last2=Tao |first2=Lei}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.umsystem.edu/stories/innovation_management_research |title=UMKC Ranks Number One for Innovation Management Research |publisher=[[University of Missouri]] |accessdate=22 March 2015}}</ref> However, the methodology of the study and the independence of its authors was questioned.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.kansascity.com/news/local/article811395.html |title=UMKC's misleading march to the top |work=[[Kansas City Star]] |accessdate=22 March 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://chronicle.com/blogs/ticker/for-business-schools-no-1-ranking-big-asterisk-looms/82737?cid=at |title=For Business School's No. 1 Ranking, Big Asterisk Looms – The Ticker - Blogs |work=[[The Chronicle of Higher Education]] |accessdate=22 March 2015}}</ref> In March, 2015, the journal published an "expression of concern" regarding the study. However, four independent scholars had later reviewed the article and found its methodology to be acceptable.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.kansascity.com/news/local/article15170036.html |title=Journal expresses concern about study that ranked UMKC No. 1 |work=[[Kansas City Star]] |accessdate=22 March 2015}}</ref>

The School is also home to a number of centers and institutes such as the [[L.P. Cookingham Institute of Urban Affairs]] and the [[Midwest Center for Nonprofit Leadership]].

<ref>[https://poetsandquants.com/2015/02/02/bloch-school-kicked-out-of-ranking/ "Bloch School Kicked Out Of Ranking"]</ref><ref>[https://www.chronicle.com/blogs/ticker/jp/princeton-review-strips-missouri-university-of-its-controversial-ranking "Princeton Review Strips Missouri University of Its Controversial Ranking"]</ref><ref>[https://www.kansascity.com/news/local/article8946158.html "UMKC loses its top rankings in the Princeton Review"]</ref><ref>[https://www.kansascity.com/news/local/article811474.html "Exaggerations mar UMKC applications for Princeton Review rankings"]</ref> The scandal included ridiculous denials by administrators from the deans to the chancellor.<ref>[https://poetsandquants.com/2015/01/31/the-sad-truth-behind-a-rankings-scandal-at-the-bloch-school-of-management/ "The Sad Truth Behind A Rankings Scandal At The Bloch School of Management"]</ref><ref>[https://www.kansascity.com/news/local/article811395.html "UMKC’s misleading march to the top"]</ref><ref>[https://www.kansascity.com/news/local/article9640337.html "UMKC chancellor apologizes for use of flawed data in pursuit of rankings"]</ref> And, the scandal even resulted in the bloating of deficits to pay for questionable programs and outrageous salaries and travel expenses and nepotistic contracts and hiring within the school.<ref>[https://poetsandquants.com/2015/02/06/the-400k-professor-at-the-center-of-the-bloch-school-scandal/2/ "The $400K Professor At The Center Of The Bloch School Scandal"]</ref><ref>[https://www.chronicle.com/blogs/ticker/jp/business-school-that-chased-rankings-ran-up-a-deficit-audit-finds "Business School That Chased Rankings Ran Up a Deficit, Audit Finds"]</ref> Two partial audits by [[PricewaterhouseCoopers]] even identified culprits and instances of misappropriated funds but the administration never punished any of those involved, some of whom remain at exorbitant salaries, or even attempted to claw back funds from cheated taxpayers.<ref>[https://www.umsystem.edu/media/curator/PWCreport.pdf?mod=article_inline "PwC Partial Audit"]</ref><ref>[https://www.kansascity.com/news/local/article840149.html "Gov. Jay Nixon calls for an inquiry into UMKC business school rankings"]</ref> While two of the main culprits left, the administration still has not told the public the true nature of their removal even while telling their accreditors a different story.<ref>[https://www.kansascity.com/news/local/article10136273.html "Amid rankings scandal, Michael Song resigns from UMKC"
]</ref><ref>[https://www.chronicle.com/blogs/ticker/professor-at-center-of-rankings-scandal-resigns/94175 "Professor at Center of Rankings Scandal in Missouri Resigns"]</ref><ref>[https://www.kansascity.com/news/local/article10772147.html "Second Bloch School faculty member resigns in wake of rankings scandal"]</ref> This joke of an attempt at donor-pressured academic credibility even made the [[Wall Street Journal]]<ref>[https://www.wsj.com/articles/do-business-school-rankings-matter-1425517222 "Do Business-School Rankings Matter?"]</ref> but has had little effect on the long-term administration of the school.<ref>[https://www.kansascity.com/opinion/editorials/article8960324.html "Princeton Review’s rankings downgrade damages UMKC’s reputation"]</ref><ref>[https://www.kansascity.com/opinion/editorials/article9633965.html "UMKC learns hard lesson about college rankings"]</ref><ref[https://www.kansascity.com/news/local/article12525209.html "Students ask UMKC chancellor more questions about the Bloch School controversy"]</ref>

A second and related ranking fraud involved a 2012 study, not peer-reviewed, published in the ''[[Journal of Product Innovation Management]]'' that hilariously ranked the school number 1 in the world for research in [[innovation management]].<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1111/j.1540-5885.2011.00898.x |title=Perspective: Ranking of the World's Top Innovation Management Scholars and Universities |journal=Journal of Product Innovation Management |volume=29 |issue=2 |pages=319 |year=2012 |last1=Yang |first1=Pianpian |last2=Tao |first2=Lei}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.umsystem.edu/stories/innovation_management_research |title=UMKC Ranks Number One for Innovation Management Research |publisher=[[University of Missouri]] |accessdate=22 March 2015}}</ref> However, the methodology of the study and the independence of its authors was questioned.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.kansascity.com/news/local/article811395.html |title=UMKC's misleading march to the top |work=[[Kansas City Star]] |accessdate=22 March 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://chronicle.com/blogs/ticker/for-business-schools-no-1-ranking-big-asterisk-looms/82737?cid=at&utm_source=at&utm_medium=en |title=For Business School's No. 1 Ranking, Big Asterisk Looms – The Ticker - Blogs |work=[[The Chronicle of Higher Education]] |accessdate=22 March 2015}}</ref> In March, 2015, the journal published an "expression of concern" regarding the study.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.kansascity.com/news/local/article15170036.html |title=Journal expresses concern about study that ranked UMKC No. 1 |work=[[Kansas City Star]] |accessdate=22 March 2015}}</ref> The study was partly written by the culprit of the Princeton Review fraud in an arrangement with the journal’s then-editor who was assured that he and his institution would also rank highly; UMKC has yet to provide that documentation to the journal in order for the full retraction to occur.<ref>[https://www.kansascity.com/news/local/article9463514.html "Bloch School leader: No. 1 ranking lacked credibility"]</ref>

A third related rankings fraud involves the United States Association for Small Business and Entrepreneurship (USASBE). At least one USASBE award for entrepreneurship programming that was based on the same (and worse) false reporting that buttressed the Princeton Review rankings. While the administration never took steps to investigate or return the reward, the faculty voted by majority to return it. USASBE’s investigation, prompted by a whistle-blower, strangely came back ‘clean’, as the school then hired the then-president of USASBE who oversaw that investigation.<ref>[https://www.kansascity.com/news/local/article9366890.html "Professor calls on UMKC to return another Bloch School honor"]</ref>

This is a school that paid one dean a base salary of half-a-million dollars, with no dean experience, no publications, and on a part-time basis.<ref>[https://www.kansascity.com/news/local/article20791836.html "Teng-Kee Tan, former dean of the Bloch School of Management, dies"]</ref> It then followed up by retaining an interim dean who was involved in the rankings fraud even after an international search for a new dean provided three viable candidates, but only after the hiring committee met with the named donor while the stories of the frauds and the reasons for the new building were being discussed.<ref>[https://www.kansascity.com/news/local/article102374157.html "UMKC Bloch School search for a new dean is underway"]</ref> In the transition, the students and taxpayers were paying two people over $400,000 each to play dean, both of whom were involved in the rankings scandals and continued to mislead the public on the underlying facts and outcomes.

The School is also home to a number of centers and institutes such as the [[L.P. Cookingham Institute of Urban Affairs]] and the [[Midwest Center for Nonprofit Leadership]].
